title: Aug 2024
des: Oman Pearson VUE paediatrics recall, August 2024. Answers checked and explained (several recall keys corrected).

questions.question: A test is done on 200 patients known to have a disease, and 180 test positive. Which statement is true?
questions.exp: Sensitivity = true positives / all with disease = 180/200 = 90%. Specificity and predictive values cannot be calculated without data on people who do not have the disease.

questions.question: Which is a recognised side effect of surfactant therapy?
questions.exp: Rapidly falling pulmonary resistance after surfactant can increase ductal left-to-right shunt and cause pulmonary haemorrhage; transient desaturation during dosing and air leak (if ventilation is not weaned) also occur.

questions.question: A child with sickle cell anaemia has fever and has been given ceftriaxone. What is the cause of his susceptibility to serious infection?
questions.exp: Repeated splenic infarction causes functional asplenia early in life, so encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus most commonly) cause sepsis and meningitis. Every febrile child with sickle cell disease needs urgent assessment, blood culture and IV ceftriaxone.

questions.question: A child with sickle cell anaemia has a fever of 40°C, and a blood culture is taken. What is the commonest organism causing bacteraemia?
questions.exp: Pneumococcus is the leading cause of bacteraemia and meningitis in sickle cell disease, despite penicillin prophylaxis and vaccination; Salmonella is a classic cause of osteomyelitis, and Hib is now rare after vaccination.

questions.question: A child with AIDS has fever, tachypnoea, tachycardia, nasal flaring and bilateral crackles. The chest X-ray shows bilateral perihilar infiltrates. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is the commonest AIDS-defining illness in infants: hypoxia, tachypnoea and diffuse perihilar or ground-glass infiltrates with few signs. Treat with IV co-trimoxazole for 21 days plus prednisolone if hypoxic, then secondary prophylaxis.

questions.question: A child with cystic fibrosis has a chest infection with Pseudomonas that does not respond to antibiotics proven effective by culture. What should be done?
questions.b: Change to meropenem without further tests
questions.c: Check total IgE and Aspergillus-specific IgE
questions.exp: Wheeze and deterioration despite appropriate antibiotics in CF suggest allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis: total IgE over 500 IU/mL, Aspergillus IgE/IgG, eosinophilia and new infiltrates. Treat with oral steroids and itraconazole.

questions.question: In antenatal screening at 19 weeks, the maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein is raised. Which condition does this suggest?
questions.b: An open neural tube defect such as spina bifida or anencephaly
questions.exp: Raised maternal AFP: open neural tube defects (anencephaly, open spina bifida), abdominal wall defects (gastroschisis, omphalocele), multiple pregnancy, wrong dates or fetal death. LOW AFP is linked to Down syndrome and trisomy 18. Follow up with a detailed anomaly scan.

questions.question: A pregnant woman has poorly controlled diabetes. Which fetal malformation is most specifically associated?
questions.exp: Caudal regression (sacral agenesis) is rare but most strongly linked to maternal diabetes; congenital heart disease and neural tube defects are more common overall. Risk rises with HbA1c in early pregnancy.

questions.question: An antenatal scan shows unilateral hydronephrosis over 10 mm with normal kidney echogenicity. After delivery the baby feeds well and passes urine. What should be done?
questions.a: Renal scan with DMSA at birth
questions.c: Renal ultrasound after 72 hours of life
questions.exp: Postnatal ultrasound is done after 48–72 hours, because early scans underestimate dilatation. Urgent scans are for bilateral dilatation, a single kidney or suspected urethral valves.

questions.question: A girl has haematuria with red cells over 100 per high-power field. History and examination are normal. What is the next investigation?
questions.exp: Isolated haematuria: confirm on repeat urine microscopy, look at red cell morphology, check BP, renal function, urine calcium:creatinine, and do an ultrasound for stones, cysts, tumours or structural problems. Biopsy only with proteinuria, hypertension or falling kidney function.

questions.question: A boy has fever, a rash and a low C4. Which investigations are needed?
questions.exp: Fever with rash and low complement suggests lupus (or immune complex disease, infective endocarditis or post-infectious GN). Check ANA, anti-dsDNA, C3, urine, and blood cultures to exclude infection.

questions.question: A child has a firm, rubbery, non-tender supraclavicular lymph node over 2.5 cm with fever and night sweats. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: A supraclavicular node is always abnormal and highly suspicious of malignancy, especially when large, firm, rubbery and with B symptoms. Do a chest X-ray, FBC, LDH and excision biopsy.

questions.question: A 7-year-old has Down syndrome. Which health surveillance is recommended?
questions.a: Ask about symptoms of obstructive sleep apnoea at every visit and test accordingly
questions.exp: Down syndrome surveillance: thyroid function every year, hearing every 1–2 years, eye checks every 1–2 years, screening for coeliac symptoms, and asking about snoring and OSA at every visit (polysomnography by 4 years in many guidelines). Echo is done in infancy; repeat only if indicated.

questions.question: When does a healthy baby double his birth weight?
questions.exp: Birth weight doubles by about 4–5 months and triples by 12 months.

questions.question: What is a benefit of delaying cord clamping for 30–60 seconds in preterm babies?
questions.exp: Delayed cord clamping in preterm babies improves blood pressure and blood volume, reduces transfusions, IVH and NEC, and lowers mortality.

questions.question: A child has skin abscesses, lymphadenitis after BCG vaccination and a liver abscess. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: CGD: recurrent abscesses (skin, liver, lymph nodes), infections with catalase-positive organisms, and BCG complications (BCG-itis). DHR test confirms.

questions.question: A child has chronic diarrhoea, persistent candida infection and failure to thrive. Which defect is most likely?
questions.b: Low T cells (severe combined or T-cell immunodeficiency)
questions.exp: Persistent thrush, chronic diarrhoea, failure to thrive and opportunistic infections in infancy suggest SCID. Lymphopenia is a clue; TRECs and lymphocyte subsets confirm. Avoid live vaccines and give irradiated blood products; stem cell transplant is curative.

questions.question: A child with CAH receives hydrocortisone. Which statement is true?
questions.a: Too little hydrocortisone slows bone maturation
questions.b: Too much hydrocortisone causes tall final height
questions.c: Growth is unaffected by the dose
questions.d: Too much hydrocortisone speeds up bone maturation
questions.e: Too little hydrocortisone speeds up growth and bone maturation
questions.exp: Under-treatment lets adrenal androgens advance growth and bone age (short final height); over-treatment suppresses growth and causes cushingoid features.

questions.question: A child has rickets, and his mother also had rickets. Calcium is normal, phosphate low and ALP high. What should be done?
questions.e: Tell the family there is a 25% risk to each child
questions.exp: Familial hypophosphataemic rickets (most often X-linked dominant, PHEX) is diagnosed by renal phosphate wasting (low TmP/GFR) with normal or low 1,25-vitamin D and high FGF23.

questions.question: A fully vaccinated 6-year-old girl stepped on a nail. The wound is dirty and bleeding. What is needed?
questions.e: Clean and debride the wound; no tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin is needed if her last dose was under 5 years ago
questions.exp: A fully immunised child with a last dose within 5 years (or 10 years in some schedules) needs only wound care. Give a booster if the last dose is older, and immunoglobulin if immunisation is incomplete or unknown and the wound is high risk.

questions.question: A child had hives on eating egg. What is the advice about the influenza vaccine?
questions.a: Give only an inactivated intramuscular vaccine in hospital
questions.e: Give the influenza vaccine as normal
questions.exp: Egg allergy is not a contraindication to influenza vaccination; give it normally in primary care.

questions.question: A boy has frequent falls and calf hypertrophy. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
questions.e: Genetic testing of the dystrophin gene
questions.exp: In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, CK is a screening test; dystrophin gene testing confirms (deletion/duplication analysis, then sequencing).

questions.question: A boy with Duchenne muscular dystrophy on long-term steroids is referred to an endocrinologist because of a complication of the drug. What is likely to be given?
questions.exp: Long-term corticosteroids in DMD cause osteoporosis with vertebral and long-bone fractures. Monitor bone density and spine X-rays; give vitamin D and calcium, and IV bisphosphonates for fractures or low bone density. Testosterone is given for delayed puberty.

questions.question: A 2-week-old bottle-fed baby takes only 30 mL, falls asleep without finishing, then wakes up and cries. What is the most likely problem?
questions.b: The teat hole is too small
questions.c: The mother made up the formula wrongly
questions.d: The mother did not burp him
questions.exp: A baby who tires quickly and sleeps without finishing feeds, then wakes hungry, has a poor or weak suck; look for prematurity, illness (sepsis, heart disease), hypotonia, or tongue-tie. A teat hole that is too small causes prolonged feeding with frustration.

questions.question: A breastfed 2-month-old's mother asks about supplements. Which one is recommended?
questions.exp: All breastfed babies need 400 IU (10 micrograms) of vitamin D daily from birth; formula-fed babies taking over 500 mL a day get enough from formula. Iron is added for preterm babies.

questions.question: A girl has features of hyperthyroidism. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Propylthiouracil is better than methimazole in children
questions.d: Radioiodine is first-line in young children
questions.e: Carbimazole (methimazole) is first-line; propylthiouracil is avoided because of liver failure
questions.exp: Carbimazole or methimazole is first-line for Graves disease in children. Both thionamides can cause agranulocytosis (warn about sore throat and fever). Propylthiouracil carries a risk of fatal liver failure and is avoided except in the first trimester of pregnancy or thyroid storm.

questions.question: An 11-year-old girl has no signs of puberty. Her mother (150 cm) had puberty at 14 years, her father normal puberty, and her bone age is 10 years. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.c: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
questions.exp: A late-maturing parent and a mildly delayed bone age suggest constitutional delay. In girls, puberty is delayed only if there is no breast development by 13 years, so this girl is still within normal limits. Check growth velocity and consider a karyotype if growth is poor.

questions.question: A 13-year-old boy is still prepubertal (SMR 1), with a normal history and examination. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Constitutional delay is the commonest cause of delayed puberty in boys. Puberty is delayed if there is no testicular enlargement by 14 years. Investigate further (LH, FSH, testosterone, bone age, smell) if over 14 or with red flags.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy has precocious puberty: testes 7 mL, penis 10 cm, pubic hair SMR 4. LH and FSH are low, testosterone is high and hCG is raised. What is the cause?
questions.b: Peripheral precocious puberty from an hCG-secreting germ cell tumour
questions.e: Central precocious puberty from a pituitary adenoma
questions.exp: Suppressed LH and FSH mean peripheral puberty; a raised hCG means an hCG-secreting germ cell tumour (pineal or suprasellar, mediastinal, hepatoblastoma), which stimulates testes through LH receptors. CAH gives small testes and high 17-OHP.

questions.question: Which statement about DKA management is correct?
questions.c: Continue the insulin infusion until ketosis has cleared, adding IV glucose as needed
questions.d: Give an insulin bolus at the start
questions.e: Stop insulin when glucose reaches 14 mmol/L
questions.exp: Insulin 0.05–0.1 units/kg/hour (BSPED 2021 suggests 0.05–0.1) continues until ketones and pH normalise; add dextrose when glucose falls rather than stopping insulin.

questions.question: A child has recurrent kidney stones, with cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine in the urine. Which statement is true?
questions.b: It is autosomal recessive and treated with hydration, urine alkalinisation and thiol drugs
questions.exp: Cystinuria (about 1 in 7,000) is autosomal recessive. Treat with high fluid intake, alkalinisation (potassium citrate), low salt, and tiopronin or penicillamine. Cysteamine treats cystinosis, a different disease.

questions.question: After a sore throat, a child develops facial swelling, dark urine and hypertension. What is the first treatment for the hypertension?
questions.d: Furosemide with fluid and salt restriction
questions.exp: Post-streptococcal GN hypertension comes from fluid overload, so a loop diuretic and fluid restriction are first; add a calcium channel blocker or hydralazine if BP stays high.

questions.question: In refeeding syndrome, which electrolyte falls first?
questions.exp: Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome, usually within 2–5 days of starting feeds.

questions.question: A girl with anorexia nervosa is admitted because of bradycardia. Which other finding is likely?
questions.exp: Starvation causes bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, cold peripheries, prolonged QTc, lanugo hair and constipation.

questions.question: What is the most common skin lesion in Crohn's disease?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum is the commonest skin manifestation of IBD (more in Crohn's), often with active disease. Pyoderma gangrenosum is rarer and more linked to UC.

questions.question: A child has hepatosplenomegaly, and liver biopsy shows lipid-laden storage cells. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.exp: Gaucher disease is caused by glucocerebrosidase deficiency, with storage cells in liver, spleen and marrow. Treat type 1 with enzyme replacement.

questions.question: A baby born at 26 weeks has been in the neonatal unit for 8 weeks. When should the hexavalent vaccine be given?
questions.b: Now, at 2 months chronological age, while still in hospital
questions.exp: Preterm babies are immunised by chronological age, with apnoea monitoring for 48–72 hours after the first dose in very preterm babies.

questions.question: A child has 3 episodes a year of fever and joint pain, with high white cells during attacks and normal health between them. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Recurrent short febrile attacks with serositis or arthritis and normal health between attacks are typical of FMF; colchicine prevents attacks and amyloidosis.

questions.question: A child with fever has a vibratory systolic murmur at the left sternal border. What is the murmur?
questions.exp: Still's murmur is a musical, vibratory systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge, louder with fever. A venous hum is continuous below the clavicles.

questions.question: What is the treatment of Kawasaki disease?
questions.exp: IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin within 10 days of fever onset; steroids are added for high-risk or resistant cases.

questions.question: What advice should be given at discharge after Kawasaki disease treatment on aspirin?
questions.c: Stop aspirin as soon as fever resolves
questions.exp: Aspirin with influenza or varicella risks Reye syndrome, so annual inactivated influenza vaccine is advised. Live vaccines are delayed 11 months after IVIG.

questions.question: A neonate has conjunctivitis, and the Gram stain shows Gram-negative diplococci. What is the organism?
questions.exp: Gonococcal ophthalmia presents at 2–5 days with heavy purulent discharge; treat with single-dose ceftriaxone.

questions.question: A 3-day-old has purulent conjunctivitis. What is the most important treatment?
questions.exp: Presumed gonococcal conjunctivitis needs systemic ceftriaxone with saline irrigation.

questions.question: After a viral URTI, a child has a petechial rash on the legs and a low platelet count. He is otherwise well. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: ITP: a well child with isolated thrombocytopenia and bruising or petechiae after a viral illness, with a normal blood film otherwise. Most recover within months; observe if no significant bleeding.

questions.question: Which central venous line site has the highest infection risk?
questions.b: Umbilical vein for less than 7 days
questions.d: Peripherally inserted central catheter in the arm
questions.exp: Femoral lines have higher rates of infection and thrombosis than subclavian lines in adults; in children the difference is smaller, but femoral sites are still avoided for long-term use when possible.

questions.question: A ventilated child develops a pneumothorax. Which ventilator change increases the risk?
questions.exp: Overdistension from high tidal volumes or pressures (and gas trapping from short expiratory times) causes air leaks.

questions.question: A 4-year-old was briefly submerged and now has a cough and has vomited. He is stable with BP 110/80. What should be done?
questions.exp: Observe at least 6–8 hours after a drowning incident; lung injury may develop later.

questions.question: A child with Alagille syndrome, lost to follow-up, comes with a large thigh haematoma after minor trauma. What is the cause?
questions.exp: Alagille syndrome (JAG1, bile duct paucity) causes chronic cholestasis with fat malabsorption, so vitamin K deficiency causes a prolonged PT and bleeding. Children with cholestasis need A, D, E and K supplements and regular INR checks.

questions.question: A boy bleeds after circumcision. APTT is prolonged and PT and TT are normal. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Isolated APTT prolongation with bleeding in a boy suggests haemophilia A (or B).

questions.question: An adolescent boy has died in the emergency department and his family was not there. How should they be told?
questions.a: Let a nurse tell them in the waiting area
questions.c: In a private room, sitting down, after a warning that there is bad news
questions.d: Ask the police to inform them
questions.exp: Senior doctor, private room, sitting down, warning shot, clear language, time and support.

questions.question: An adolescent girl has moderate to severe depression on a questionnaire. What is the first step?
questions.a: Ask about self-harm and suicidal ideas
questions.b: Start fluoxetine immediately without further assessment
questions.exp: Risk assessment comes first in any young person with depression: ask directly about self-harm and suicidal thoughts, plans and means. Then psychological therapy, with fluoxetine for moderate to severe depression.

questions.question: Which is an important side effect of SSRIs in young people?
questions.a: Severe withdrawal so they must never be stopped
questions.e: Increased suicidal thoughts, especially early in treatment
questions.exp: SSRIs can increase suicidal thinking and agitation in under-25s, especially in the first weeks; review closely. Stop gradually to avoid discontinuation symptoms.

questions.question: A child took amitriptyline and has a dry mouth and a QRS over 140 ms. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Sodium bicarbonate narrows the QRS and prevents arrhythmias in tricyclic poisoning.

questions.question: A 2-week-old has respiratory distress, and the chest X-ray shows a "figure of 8" heart. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Supracardiac TAPVR causes the "snowman" or figure-of-8 heart.

questions.question: A child has a skin rash on the hands and muscle weakness. Which complication is associated?
questions.exp: Juvenile dermatomyositis (Gottron papules, heliotrope rash, proximal weakness) is complicated by calcinosis in up to 40%.

questions.question: An asthmatic on oral steroids and high-dose inhalers still has symptoms and a history of allergy. What is the management?
questions.e: Check IgE and consider anti-IgE therapy (omalizumab)
questions.exp: Severe allergic asthma at GINA step 5 with raised IgE can be treated with omalizumab.

questions.question: A 2-year-old girl has had delayed gross motor development since 6 months and delayed speech. What is the initial test?
questions.exp: Global delay: start with hearing and vision and a full examination; first-line genetic tests and others as indicated.

questions.question: A 2-month-old's mother is worried about a squint. The red reflex is absent. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Squint with absent red reflex (leukocoria) means urgent referral to exclude retinoblastoma; cataract is the other main cause.

questions.question: Which statement about ROP is true?
questions.a: It is caused by low oxygen only
questions.c: It is a preventable cause of blindness
questions.exp: Screening and timely treatment prevent most blindness from ROP; oxygen saturation targeting helps prevent it.

questions.question: A ventilated child develops post-extubation stridor from airway oedema. What can prevent it?
questions.d: Dexamethasone before extubation and for several doses after
questions.exp: Dexamethasone given 6–12 hours before and after extubation reduces post-extubation stridor in high-risk children.

questions.question: A child has purpura, haemolytic anaemia with fragmented red cells, splenomegaly and a raised creatinine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Microangiopathic haemolysis (fragments), thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury in a child is usually HUS (often after STEC diarrhoea). TTP (ADAMTS13 deficiency) is rare in children and adds fever and neurological signs.

questions.question: A girl has coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, hyperactivity and developmental regression. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.b: A mucopolysaccharidosis (such as Sanfilippo, MPS III)
questions.exp: Coarse features with organomegaly suggest a storage disorder; marked hyperactivity and regression with relatively mild physical signs are typical of Sanfilippo syndrome. Test urinary glycosaminoglycans and enzymes.

questions.question: A father passes his disease to 50% of his children, whatever the partner. Which disease fits?
questions.exp: A 50% risk from one parent to children of either sex is autosomal dominant (NF1).

questions.question: An infant has irritability, jaundice, failure to thrive, a high alpha-fetoprotein and coagulopathy. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Tyrosinaemia type 1: liver failure with coagulopathy, very high AFP, renal tubulopathy and rickets; succinylacetone in urine or blood is diagnostic. Treat with nitisinone.

questions.question: A new IV fluid is tested to see whether it causes iatrogenic hyponatraemia, with children randomly given it or the standard fluid. What type of study is this?
questions.exp: When the investigator assigns the treatment by randomisation and compares outcomes, it is an RCT.

questions.question: A child speaks in 3-word sentences, knows his name and walks up and down stairs with alternating feet. What is his age?
questions.exp: At 3 years: 3-word sentences, knows name and age, alternate feet going upstairs, rides a tricycle, copies a circle. At 2 years: 2-word phrases, two feet per step.

questions.question: Which skin finding is typical of niacin deficiency?
questions.a: Acrodermatitis around the mouth and nappy area
questions.b: A photosensitive dermatitis (such as Casal necklace)
questions.exp: Pellagra: photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia.

questions.question: A neonate has firm red-purple plaques on the back. Which complication is associated?
questions.exp: Subcutaneous fat necrosis can cause delayed hypercalcaemia; monitor calcium for months.

questions.question: A baby was born after a placental abruption with severe hypotonia and bilateral miosis (moderate encephalopathy). What may improve the outcome?
questions.exp: Moderate to severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy in babies of 36 weeks or more: whole-body cooling to 33–34°C for 72 hours, started within 6 hours, reduces death and disability.

questions.question: A child has an anaphylactic reaction to a blood transfusion. Which condition should be suspected?
questions.exp: Patients with selective IgA deficiency can develop anti-IgA antibodies and anaphylaxis to blood products; use IgA-deficient donors or washed products.

questions.question: Burnout includes a reduced sense of effectiveness. What is this linked to?
questions.e: Low self-esteem and reduced sense of personal accomplishment
questions.exp: The three dimensions of burnout (Maslach) are emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment.

questions.question: A child has a painful testicular mass after trauma with a blue spot at the upper pole. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: The blue dot sign is a torted appendix testis; managed conservatively once testicular torsion is excluded.

questions.question: A 2-year-old has episodes of abdominal pain, drawing his knees to his chest. Two days later he vomits and passes blood in the stool. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: Intussusception: ultrasound shows a target or doughnut sign; treat with air or contrast enema reduction if no peritonitis.

questions.question: A 2-month-old with lethargy and apnoea has a rib fracture on the chest X-ray. What should be done first?
questions.exp: Lethargy and apnoea in an infant with signs of abuse suggest abusive head trauma, so urgent CT brain is needed first, followed by skeletal survey, eye exam and safeguarding referral.

questions.question: A child in status epilepticus did not respond to 2 doses of midazolam. What is next?
questions.b: IV sodium valproate as the first choice in all
questions.exp: After two benzodiazepine doses, give levetiracetam or phenytoin (valproate is an alternative in older children but avoided under 2 years and in suspected metabolic disease).

questions.question: A teenager took aspirin in a suicide attempt 45 minutes ago. What is the management?
questions.e: A single dose of activated charcoal
questions.exp: Charcoal within 1 hour, salicylate levels, alkalinisation and psychiatric assessment.

questions.question: An infant has low sodium and potassium and recurrent pneumonia, with no consanguinity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Salt depletion with metabolic alkalosis and chest infections in infancy suggests CF; confirm with a sweat test.

questions.question: The infant of a vegan mother has a macrocytic anaemia. What is deficient?
questions.exp: Exclusively breastfed infants of vegan mothers who do not supplement can develop B12 deficiency with macrocytic anaemia and neurological problems.

questions.question: Which is the most important risk factor for sudden infant death syndrome?
questions.exp: Prenatal smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor along with prone sleeping; dummies, room-sharing and breastfeeding are protective.

questions.question: A 1-month-old has congenital muscular torticollis. What is the management?
questions.a: Refer to physiotherapy for a stretching programme
questions.exp: Congenital muscular torticollis (sternocleidomastoid fibrosis or tumour) is treated with early physiotherapy and positioning; most resolve within a year. Refer to orthopaedics if not improving by 6–12 months. Exclude ocular torticollis (squint) and hip dysplasia.

questions.question: A boy has jaundice and splenomegaly. His father and uncle had cholecystectomies when young. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Autosomal dominant haemolysis with splenomegaly and early gallstones in family members suggests hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.question: A child has hives and respiratory distress after exposure to an allergen. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Skin features plus breathing problems = anaphylaxis: give IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg.

questions.question: A child with sickle cell anaemia not on hydroxyurea develops hemiplegia. What should be done?
questions.exp: Acute stroke in sickle cell disease needs urgent exchange (or top-up) transfusion after imaging, then long-term transfusion.

questions.question: A patient with tuberous sclerosis has an MRI brain. Which tumour is typical?
questions.exp: SEGA arises near the foramen of Monro in tuberous sclerosis and can cause hydrocephalus; mTOR inhibitors (everolimus) shrink it.
